agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: The crash was a bug on my side: every answer opens with either "Let" or "Here", so the third category was empty. That's a useful fact in itself, because the very first token picks one of two modes. The Let mode scores 30.2% on finished answers, and the Here mode 17.7%. This gap is large but could still reflect which problems go to which mode, so I'll treat it as a hypothesis for now. I'll rerun the layer analysis without the empty category. I'll also check whether the mode can be read from the last prompt token, and whether cut-versus-finished differences show up there or only during the answer.
That was also my error. `tstat` was defined after the line that crashed, so it never got created. Here's the same analysis with the helper defined first.

Looping shows up strongly during the answer, with |t| up to 56 and thousands of neurons from layers 5-16. It's only weakly visible at the last prompt token (|t| ≤ 8), so it develops during generation and isn't set in advance by the problem. Answer mode behaves differently: it's readable at the last prompt token, and its separation grows from layer 4 to about |t|=27 in the late layers. So a clear early decision may steer the rest of the answer. Correct-versus-wrong barely separates, with |t| around 5-7 across 6,912 neurons (close to the chance maximum), which is what I'd expect if failures aren't one simple unit. Before investing in mode, I want to know whether its gap reflects problem difficulty. Without using a pass, I'll stratify accuracy by reference solution length (number of steps) and problem length, and check whether Let answers actually restate the facts before calculating. I'll also read a few Let-mode loops to see what they look like at the point they fail to terminate. If Let beats Here within each difficulty stratum, the mode effect becomes a credible causal candidate. If the gap vanishes, I'll drop it.

Mode survives the difficulty control. Let beats Here in every step stratum up to 4 steps (48% vs 27%, 35% vs 20%, 23% vs 10% on finished answers), and the stratified difference is +7.4 points in overall accuracy, even though Let has more cut-offs. That's a credible causal candidate, though only an intervention can show that flipping a "Here" problem to Let actually helps. Conveniently, the mode is decided at a single, highly recognisable position: the token right after `<start_of_turn>model\n`. That suggests a clean test: find an MLP neuron that's strongly and near-constantly active at that position and quiet elsewhere, then have it write the Let-minus-Here direction. I can screen for such neurons with the stored summaries (last-prompt versus answer-mean activity) at no pass cost. Finding selective, low-variance neurons would confirm this is feasible as a narrow edit. I'd then confirm their token-level silence with a teacher-forced pass before building anything.
